---
title: 'Extraction Methodology'
subtitle: 'How chapter PDFs become minimal HTML'
---

## Typography as structure

The Stadt.Geschichte.Basel series uses one consistent typographic system across all nine volumes. Because every kind of content is set in a distinct font and size, each line of the PDF text layer can be classified by the font and size of its dominant span — no machine learning, no heuristics on wording, just the design system itself:

| Font and size                        | Meaning                                    | Treatment                 |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------- |
| EuclidCircularB-Semibold ≥ 18 pt     | chapter title                              | cross-check with OMP      |
| EuclidCircularB-Semibold ~14 pt      | section headings                           | `<h2>`                    |
| EuclidCircularB-Regular ~14 pt       | author line on the opener                  | sets the author order, then dropped |
| EuclidCircularB-Regular ~12.5 pt     | lead (intro) paragraph                     | `<p class="lead">`        |
| Practice ~10.4 pt                    | body text (Italic → `<em>`)                | `<p>`                     |
| Practice-Extrabold ~11 pt            | pull quotes (duplicated design text)       | dropped                   |
| EuclidCircularB-Semibold ~9.5 pt     | sidebar/inset headings                     | `<h3>` in `<aside>`       |
| EuclidCircularB-Regular ~8.5 pt      | sidebar/inset prose                        | `<aside>`                 |
| EuclidCircularB ~7–7.5 pt            | captions, running heads, page numbers      | dropped                   |
| EuclidCircularB ~6.5 pt              | endnote text                               | `<section>` of `<ol>`     |
| Practice-Bold < 6 pt, superscript    | footnote markers in running text           | `<sup><a href="#fn…">`    |

Lines in fonts foreign to the series (e.g. Helvetica) are OCR layers inside reproduced historical images and are dropped with a warning. Unknown sizes of the series fonts fail open into the body text and are logged for review.

## Text reconstruction

- **De-hyphenation** — the PDFs mark hyphenation breaks with soft hyphens (U+00AD): a line ending in a soft hyphen joins the next line without a space; a hard hyphen at a line end is a broken compound (`rot-blaue`) and is kept; an en dash before a digit continues a number range (`S. 123–127`).
- **Paragraphs across pages** — paragraphs are detected by first-line indents (~25–30 pt) and continue across page breaks and around floated boxes (larger x-shifts of ~60 pt are text flowing around pull quotes or images, not new paragraphs).
- **Endnotes** — the `Anmerkungen` section is set in two or three columns; lines are re-ordered column by column, note starts are recognized by their bold number spans, and markers are matched to notes by number (sidebar notes continue the chapter numbering; duplicate numbers are disambiguated by occurrence order).
- **Footnote markers vs. superscripts** — only *bold* superscript digits are markers; regular superscripts such as the isotope notation ¹⁴C stay plain text.
- **Sidebar paragraphs** — sidebar text has no indents, so a short line that ends a sentence ends the paragraph; abbreviations and closing quotation marks do not count.
- **Tables, maps, and charts** — tables are not part of the edition. Text from maps and charts (labels with digits, capitals, or repeated words) is dropped.
- **Figure anchors** — inline references like `[7 | 8]` point to images that are not part of the edition and are removed together with the figures, captions, and pull quotes.

## Authors and author order

The OMP API gives the author names of a chapter. It does not give a usable order. By default every author has position 0, so OMP shows the authors in random order until an administrator sets the order.

The converter takes the order from the printed book. It uses the first source that names all authors of the chapter:

1. The author line on the first page of the chapter PDF.
2. One line in the first 12 pages of the volume PDF that holds all names, for example "Herausgegeben von A und B".
3. The printed contents of the volume. The contents list each article with its authors. The converter orders the authors by their first article.
4. Alphabetical order by family name.

A line break between two names means a list, not an author line. The converter ignores such a match. For example, a title page can list all authors alphabetically.

The author line of the chapter has priority over the contents. The contents list articles. An article can have a different first author than the chapter.

Volumes 8 and 9 print no author line on their chapter pages. Volume 9 lists the authors of each article in its contents. Volume 8 does not, so its chapters use the alphabetical order.

## Appendix chapters

Author biographies have no hanging indents. A short line or a vertical gap ends a biography. Wrapped heading lines join. Headings far apart stay separate. The extractor does not yet split image credits and index sub-entries.

Each volume's final chapter (*Anhang*) — bibliography, image credits, registers, author notes — uses a different typographic register set almost entirely in small EuclidCircularB. When a chapter contains no body text in the series' body font, the extractor switches to an appendix mode: ~9.5 pt Semibold section headings, ~9 pt intro prose (split on vertical gaps), and ~6.5 pt entries with hanging indents, read column by column.

## Quality assurance

`sgb-html check` computes, per chapter:

- the **word-count ratio** of extracted text against the raw PDF text layer (typical values 0.72–0.97; the difference is dropped captions and design furniture), and
- **marker/endnote consistency** — every footnote marker must have a matching endnote.

The core modules (`extract.py`, `render.py`) are pure functions over span dictionaries and carry **100% test coverage**.

## Manual review with subagents

The extractor is deterministic. An error in one chapter is therefore an error class that can occur in other chapters. A review finds such classes. A person then fixes the extractor and never edits `html/` by hand.

`sgb-html review-pack` builds a review pack for each chapter in `.review/<doi>/`. The folder `.review/` is not under version control. A pack holds:

- `chapter.html`: a copy of the HTML, and `manifest.json`, which records the git commit.
- `pages/pNN.png`: one image for each PDF page, at 110 dpi.
- `ledger.tsv`: one row for each PDF line. It shows the role that the extractor gave to the line, and whether it kept the line. The ledger uses the same decision function as `convert`.
- `lint.json`: static findings, for example a space inside a URL.
- `diff.json`: candidates from a text comparison of the HTML with the PDF text layer. The comparison finds missing lines, extra text, swapped paragraphs, spaces inside words, and wrong endnotes. A reviewer confirms each candidate against the page image.
- `blocks.tsv`: an index of the HTML blocks, for locators such as `p#42`.

One Sonnet subagent reviews one chapter. The rubric is in `docs/chapter-review-rubric.md`. The subagent reads the pack and writes only `findings.json` in its own pack folder. Each finding quotes the HTML and the PDF. Each finding has one class from a fixed list.

Before a full run, the review must pass a recall test. A script puts 15 seeded errors into the HTML of three chapters: two body chapters and one appendix chapter. The script chooses errors that lint cannot see, for example a removed paragraph or two swapped endnotes. The review must find at least 80% of them. Use a second set of seeded errors, which nobody used to tune the tools, to confirm the result.

After a full run, a person groups the findings by class. The person checks a sample of each class against the PDF. Each verified class becomes one GitHub issue.

## Publishing to Open Monograph Press

Each chapter edition is attached to its volume's HTML publication format via the OMP 3.4 REST API (`fileStage=10`, `assocType=521`). Three undocumented quirks of the API matter:

1. `POST /submissions/{id}/files` fails with HTTP 500 if a `name` form field is included — the display name must come from the multipart filename.
2. The publication-format association (`assocType`/`assocId`/`genreId`) must be set **at upload time**; the edit endpoint rejects `assocType` changes.
3. Every `PUT`/`DELETE` on a file needs `stageId=5` (production workflow stage) as a query parameter.

The chapter link (`chapterId`), visibility, and open-access sales type are set in a second step. Uploads are idempotent: files already attached under the same name are skipped unless `--replace` is given, in which case the old galley is deleted first. A replaced galley gets a new file ID and a new download URL. Link to the chapter page, not to the file.

OMP 3.4 has no REST route for the order of chapter authors. The chapter grid is read-only while a publication is published. An OMP administrator must set the position of each author. DataCite keeps its own creator list. Its order changes only when the press updates the DOI metadata.

## Publishing to Zenodo

Each chapter and each volume has a record in the Zenodo community `stadt-geschichte-basel`. A record keeps the existing DOI `10.21255/…` and holds the PDF of the chapter or volume.

The description of a chapter record holds the HTML edition. It contains the content of `<main>` and the endnotes under the heading `Anmerkungen`. Zenodo limits the HTML:

- Zenodo removes the attributes `id`, `role`, and `value`. It also removes the elements `<aside>` and `<section>`.
- Zenodo keeps `<a name>`, `<ol>`, `<li>`, `<sup>`, and `class`. Markers and endnotes therefore use anchors such as `<a name="fn12"></a>`.
- Zenodo changes typographic quotation marks to straight marks and removes zero-width spaces. Compare the text after normalization, not the bytes.

The community uses closed review. A curator accepts the review request of a record. The acceptance publishes the record.

A published record cannot be deleted, and its PDF cannot be replaced. A curator can still edit the description, the creators, and the keywords.

## Refresh the published copies

A change to the extractor changes `html/`. The same text exists in three more places: the OMP galleys, the Zenodo records, and the website. Refresh them in this order:

1. Merge the change into `main`, then run `uv run sgb-html convert`.
2. Replace the galleys in OMP with `uv run sgb-html upload --replace --doi <DOI suffix>`.
3. Update the description and the creators of the Zenodo records.
4. Regenerate the chapter pages of the website with `scripts/generate_volumes.py` in the repository `stadt-geschichte-basel.github.io`.
5. Compare each copy with `html/`. Check the text, the number of links, and the number of endnotes.
